Two colleagues may both prepare carefully for a meeting or revise a draft several times. Training, responsibilities, and the deadline can account for those behaviors regardless of type.

T/F concerns which considerations carry weight when choosing among options. In a research project, two people can use the same evidence and give different weight to the consequences for participants and the criteria used to compare designs.

In a fictional research meeting, two colleagues review the same proposal, evidence, and review criteria. One concern is whether the study addresses a question that matters to the affected group. Another is whether the same evidentiary standard has been applied to each option. Either colleague can raise both concerns.

Two colleagues may both prepare carefully for a meeting or revise a draft several times. Training, responsibilities, and the deadline can account for those behaviors regardless of type.

Their shared I concerns attention and energy, N concerns the kinds of information they give weight to, and J concerns structure in dealings with the outside world. None of the three identifies meeting habits or research ability.

T/F concerns which considerations carry weight when choosing among options. In a research project, two people can use the same evidence and give different weight to the consequences for participants and the criteria used to compare designs.

In a fictional research meeting, two colleagues review the same proposal, evidence, and review criteria. One concern is whether the study addresses a question that matters to the affected group. Another is whether the same evidentiary standard has been applied to each option. Either colleague can raise both concerns.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Two colleagues may both prepare carefully for a meeting or revise a draft several times. Training, responsibilities, and the deadline can account for those behaviors regardless of type.

Their shared I concerns attention and energy, N concerns the kinds of information they give weight to, and J concerns structure in dealings with the outside world. None of the three identifies meeting habits or research ability.

T/F concerns which considerations carry weight when choosing among options. In a research project, two people can use the same evidence and give different weight to the consequences for participants and the criteria used to compare designs.

### INFJ and INTJ: which standard closes the direction

In a fictional research meeting, two colleagues review the same proposal, evidence, and review criteria. One concern is whether the study addresses a question that matters to the affected group. Another is whether the same evidentiary standard has been applied to each option. Either colleague can raise both concerns.

Project stage, review requirements, and available data can affect which issue needs attention. Obligations to participants and institutional requirements apply to everyone.

A worthwhile question still needs a design that can answer it. A sound design still needs a clear purpose. Treat both as part of the decision.

An INFJ can defend the reasoning behind a design, and an INTJ can ask whether a study respects participants’ priorities. Choice of argument does not measure methodological skill or concern for others.

For reflection, ask what criteria you used to choose between two viable options and what might change your mind. Speaking order, talk time, and editing speed are poor clues to T/F.

### INFJ and INTJ: why the ends stay put and the middle shifts

In type dynamics, the J in both codes identifies the outward-facing process as a judging process. Because both types are introverted, that process is auxiliary. INFJ’s auxiliary is Fe and INTJ’s is Te. Both are led by Ni, with Se in the inferior position.

In the model, Fe considers values and relationships in the outer world, while Te applies logical criteria to external decisions. The notation used here places Ti third for INFJ and Fi third for INTJ. The two stacks have different judging processes in those positions.

The Foundation lists tertiary Thinking for INFJ (Te or Ti) and tertiary Feeling for INTJ (Fe or Fi). This page uses Ti and Fi. Those alternatives leave Ni and the auxiliary process unchanged. See the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj) and [INTJ profile](/en/personality/intj) for the full descriptions.

All six rows assume the same project, evidence, review feedback, deadline, and decision authority on both sides.

Each row compares two criteria that either person can apply to the same decision. The examples illustrate possible emphases within the model.

| Same decision and evidence | INFJ: possible emphasis | INTJ: possible emphasis | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Evaluating the same paper | How much does the question matter to the people the conclusion would affect? | Does the conclusion meet the same evidentiary standard as comparable claims? | T/F: relevance to affected people and consistent criteria. Both matter. |
| Choosing between two research questions | Which option better reflects the priorities of the people involved? | Which option better meets the stated criteria when applied consistently? | T/F: people and values or consistent evaluation criteria |
| Responding to feedback that the contribution is unclear | What would the intended readers find useful about the contribution? | What contribution can be claimed under the same standard of evidence? | T/F: usefulness to people and consistency with the criteria |
| Choosing among feasible changes after a budget cut | How would each option affect participants and commitments already made? | How well does each option meet the same design and evidence criteria? | T/F: impact and commitments or consistently applied criteria |
| Choosing between two edits to a shared draft | Which version better respects readers and represents collaborators’ concerns? | Which version applies the same standard for qualifying claims across the draft? | T/F: effects on readers or consistent standards. Either person can check both. |
| Revising after a supervisor rejects the proposal | Which revision best addresses the stated concerns and the effects on the people involved? | Which revision best meets the stated review criteria when applied to all options? | T/F: consequences for people and consistent decision criteria |

Colleagues can share responsibility for choosing a direction. Discuss which criteria matter and what evidence supports each option.

### INFJ and INTJ: setting the direction, and which condition gates it

In this fictional project, two colleagues have the same data, draft question, and authority. They need to decide whether the question matters to the people affected and whether the design can support the proposed inference.

One concern is whether the people affected would recognize the question as useful. Another is whether the same limits on inference apply to both proposed designs. Either person can raise both concerns. Evaluating an inference requires attention to the design and measurements. Sample size or use of secondary data alone cannot settle that question.

Write down who might use the findings and for what decision. Then state what the design can support and which claims would go beyond the data. Assign the checks according to relevant knowledge and confirm both before deciding.

Ask each colleague to explain why they would choose one proposal over another. Compare how they weighed usefulness to people and the conditions under which the claim would hold. This exercise describes one decision and has no score or typing rule.

### INFJ and INTJ: co-writing a review, and whose paragraphs move

In this fictional review, both authors have the same draft, audience, and publication requirements. One proposed edit better acknowledges a concern readers may have. Another applies the same limits to comparable claims across the draft.

Both authors can assess how the edits affect readers and whether the claims are consistently qualified. The venue and the evidence help determine what the final draft needs.

Either author can adjust tone or revise a claim. The order of the edits does not establish T/F. Explain what the edit is meant to accomplish and which requirements it must meet.

### INFJ and INTJ: half the budget is gone, one expense sheet

In this fictional budget cut, both researchers have the same expense sheet, deadlines, and record of commitments. They compare the same feasible changes using information about costs, participant follow-ups, and each item’s role in the design.

One concern is whether an option would break a commitment to participants. Another is whether every proposed change meets the same evidentiary threshold for the main claim. Either researcher can raise both. Existing obligations still apply.

Project stage, commitments, and available data guide the decision. Assign the checks to the people who know the participant arrangements and the design, regardless of type.
